ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Diuretic foundations: 3

A clinician adds a diuretic that opposes aldosterone signaling and reduces renal potassium secretion. Which mechanism explains why this agent differs from potassium-wasting loop diuretics despite both classes promoting sodium excretion?

  1. NCC inhibition in the distal convoluted tubule
  2. ENaC blockade in the collecting system
  3. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition
  4. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism
  5. NKCC2 inhibition in the thick ascending limb
Answer and explanation

Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism

Spironolactone and eplerenone block aldosterone signaling and reduce potassium secretion.

Option explanations

Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism: Spironolactone and eplerenone block aldosterone signaling and reduce potassium secretion.

NKCC2 inhibition in the thick ascending limb: Loop diuretics inhibit sodium-potassium-chloride transport in the thick ascending limb. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

NCC inhibition in the distal convoluted tubule: Thiazides inhibit the distal sodium-chloride cotransporter. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

ENaC blockade in the collecting system: Amiloride and triamterene directly block epithelial sodium channels. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Carbonic anhydrase inhibition: Acetazolamide reduces bicarbonate reabsorption, predominantly in the proximal tubule. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
